title: The Free Coke and the Raffle Tickets
text:
At Cornell University in the late 1960s, the psychologist Dennis Regan brought students into the lab for what they thought was a study of art appreciation. Each one worked alongside a second "participant" named Joe, who was really Regan's assistant. During a short break, Joe left the room and came back with two bottles of Coca-Cola, one for himself and one for the participant, which he offered without being asked. In other sessions, Joe came back empty-handed.

Later Joe asked a favor of his own. He was selling raffle tickets at 25 cents each and would get a prize if he sold the most. Would the participant buy some? Those who had received the unasked-for Coke bought about twice as many tickets as those who had received nothing, spending well over the price of the drink.

Regan also varied how likable Joe seemed, by having him behave either pleasantly or unpleasantly during the session. Without the Coke, people who liked Joe bought more tickets. With the Coke, the gap mostly disappeared: the small gift created a sense of debt that worked even toward someone they did not much like.
lesson: Small unrequested kindnesses create a real pull to give back. Notice it when others use it on you, and use it honestly yourself by giving first without strings.
source: Regan, D. T. (1971). Effects of a favor and liking on compliance. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 7(6), 627-639.
